title: Maximum XOR Score Subarray Queries
statement:
The **XOR score** of an array is the single number left after shrinking it. In one round, every element except the last becomes the XOR of itself and the element to its right (all of them change at once, from the old values), and then the last element is deleted. Rounds repeat until one element remains, and that element is the score; an array of length 1 scores its only element.

You are given an integer array `nums` and an array `queries` with `queries[i] = [l_i, r_i]`. For each query, consider every non-empty contiguous subarray of `nums` that starts at index `l_i` or later and ends at index `r_i` or earlier, and find the largest XOR score among them. Return an array `answer` with one entry per query, where `answer[i]` is the result for `queries[i]`.
constraints: queries[i] = [l_i, r_i] with 0 <= l_i <= r_i <= n - 1
notes:
## Intuition

Playing the rounds on one subarray costs O(len²), and a range has O(len²) subarrays, so simulating every query is hopeless. The key is a link between intervals. The first round turns `nums[i..j]` into the element-wise XOR of `nums[i..j-1]` and `nums[i+1..j]`, and later rounds only XOR elements together, so the score of an element-wise XOR is the XOR of the two scores: `score(i, j) = score(i, j-1) ^ score(i+1, j)`. That is an interval DP over shorter intervals. A second quantity tracks the best score inside each interval: `best(i, j) = max(score(i, j), best(i, j-1), best(i+1, j))`, because every shorter subarray of `[i, j]` misses its first or its last element. A query `[l, r]` is then just `best(l, r)`.

## Approach

1. File every query index under its left end in `byLeft`.
2. Compute rows from `i = n - 1` down to `0`. Row `i` needs only row `i + 1`, so `score` and `best` are single arrays: before row `i`, `score[j]` and `best[j]` describe the interval `[i + 1, j]`.
3. Start row `i` with `score[i] = best[i] = nums[i]`.
4. For `j` going up from `i + 1`, `score[j - 1]` already belongs to row `i` and `score[j]` still to row `i + 1`: XOR them, then let `best[j]` be the largest of `best[j - 1]`, `best[j]` and the new score.
5. Row `i` is now complete, so every query starting at `i` reads `best[r]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 8, 4, 32, 16, 1]`; queries 0 and 2 start at index 0 and query 1 at index 1.

- Rows `i = 5` down to `2` cover the intervals starting at 2 or later. After row 2, `score[2..5]` is `4, 36, 20, 53` and `best[2..5]` is `4, 36, 48, 53`.
- Row 1: `score[1..5]` becomes `8, 12, 40, 60, 9` and `best[1..5]` becomes `8, 12, 40, 60, 60`. Query 1 (`[1, 4]`) reads `best[4] = 60`, the score of `[8, 4, 32, 16]`.
- Row 0: `score` becomes `2, 10, 6, 46, 18, 27` and `best` becomes `2, 10, 12, 46, 60, 60`. Query 0 reads `best[2] = 12` (from `[8, 4]`) and query 2 reads `best[5] = 60`.

The answer is `[12, 60, 60]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² + q): each of the n² / 2 intervals takes O(1) work and each query is read once.
- Space: O(n + q): two rows, the buckets and the answers.

## Pitfalls

- The answer is not `score(l, r)`: a shorter subarray can win. In Example 2 the range `[0, 7, 3, 2]` scores 6 as a whole, but `[7]` scores 7.
- Move `j` upward. Going downward would read `score[j - 1]` from row `i + 1` instead of row `i`.
- Two full n × n tables hold 8 million numbers; keeping one row of each and answering queries as their row finishes keeps memory at O(n + q).
- All values are below 2^31, so every XOR fits in a 32-bit `int`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `byLeft` | `byLeft[i]` lists the queries whose range starts at `i` |
| `k` | index of a query |
| `i`, `j` | the interval `[i, j]` being computed |
| `score` | `score[j]` is the XOR score of `nums[i..j]` |
| `best` | `best[j]` is the largest XOR score of a subarray inside `nums[i..j]` |
| `answer` | the result for each query |
